content: A thermodynamic process can be described as the energetic transformation of a thermodynamic system as it transitions from an initial state to a final state. The trajectory of this transformation is often defined by maintaining certain thermodynamic variables constant. These processes are frequently categorized into pairs, where each constant variable corresponds to one member of a conjugate pair. The pressure-volume conjugate pair is associated with the transfer of mechanical or dynamic energy due to work. An isobaric process occurs when the pressure remains constant. For instance, consider a cylinder with a movable piston. The pressure inside the cylinder is maintained at atmospheric pressure, even though the system is isolated from the atmosphere. This is achieved by dynamically connecting the system, via a movable boundary, to a constant-pressure reservoir. An isochoric process is one in which the volume is held constant, meaning no work is performed by the system. In such a scenario, any heat energy transferred to the system externally is entirely absorbed as internal energy. This type of process is also referred to as an isometric or isovolumetric process. A practical example would be placing a sealed tin can containing only air into a fire. The can does not expand, and the only change is an increase in the internal energy of the gas, as evidenced by a rise in its temperature and pressure. Mathematically, this is expressed as ΔQ = dU. In this case, the system is dynamically insulated from the environment by a rigid boundary. The temperature-entropy conjugate pair is concerned with the transfer of thermal energy due to heating. An isothermal process occurs at a constant temperature. For example, a system immersed in a large constant-temperature bath will maintain its temperature. Any work performed by the system will result in energy loss to the bath, but the system's temperature remains unchanged. This implies that the system is thermally connected to a constant-temperature reservoir via a thermally conductive boundary. An adiabatic process is one in which no energy is added to or removed from the system through heating or cooling. In a reversible process, this is equivalent to an isentropic process. The system is thermally insulated from its environment, with its boundary acting as a thermal insulator. If the system's entropy has not yet reached its maximum equilibrium value, the entropy will increase even though the system is thermally insulated. An isentropic process occurs at constant entropy. For a reversible process, this is identical to an adiabatic process. If the system's entropy has not yet reached its maximum equilibrium value, cooling may be required to maintain the constant entropy. Any of the thermodynamic potentials can be held constant during a process. For example: An isenthalpic process involves no change in the system's enthalpy. The above descriptions assume that the system boundaries are impermeable to particles. However, boundaries can also be rigid and thermally insulating while being permeable to one or more types of particles. In such cases, similar considerations apply to the chemical potential-particle number conjugate pairs.
